authorVisualReview: All65 diagrams inspected in six full-bank contact sheets; corrected exact catalyst peaks, explicit MB threshold, cycle state-function labels, linearised rate plot and dimensionless dilution comparison.
authorEditorialReview: Student-facing prose, concentration/temperature/energy units, formula protection, scientific notation and significant-figure reporting checked after protected-token spacing pass.
scopeNotes: R1formation/combustion-data and Born-Haber calculations confined toHL
R2initial-rate orders, Arrhenius and quantitative composition confined toHL
No quadratic equilibrium solution required; square-root-linear relations or explicitly checked approximations used
Quantitative equilibrium expressions use numerical concentrations inM; GibbsQ/Kdimensionless
All experimental/curve data constructed and marked as such; no copied past-paper questions

checks.check: Constant-pressure reaction heat has the opposite sign to calorimeter heat; extrapolation corrects heat loss, not incomplete reaction.
Relative energy levels specify ΔH; catalysts change the barrier but not reactant/product energy levels.
Fuel comparison must normalise by useful delivered energy; carbon in each fuel becomes CO2 only under complete combustion.
Calibration incorporates all heat absorbed by cup/contents; an exothermic reaction has opposite heat sign.
MgCl2 cycle requires both magnesium ionisation energies and two chlorine electron affinities; lattice formation is gaseous ions to solid.
Na2O requires two sodium atoms/ionisations, half an O2 dissociation, and both successive oxygen electron affinities, including the endothermic second affinity.
Born–Haber accounting fixes the unknown second oxygen affinity; doubly charged oppositely charged ions explain especially strong lattice attractions.
Formation-data sums must include all product coefficients; a mole fraction is inferred only after calculating both fuel combustion enthalpies.
Graphite, not every carbon allotrope, is the elemental reference standard state; diamond combustion follows Hess’s law.
Solid-to-aqueous ions can be decomposed into lattice dissociation and separate gas-ion-to-aqueous hydration steps; positive solution enthalpy cools surroundings.
Vaporisation has positive enthalpy/entropy; standard Gibbs sign compares the specified liquid and gas states at the fixed standard pressure.
For temperature-independent ΔH and ΔS, a ΔG° versus T graph has intercept ΔH° and slope −ΔS°; Gibbs-energy axes are distinct from reaction-coordinate energy profiles.
Combining ΔG°=ΔH°−TΔS° with −RTlnK at one unknown temperature does not require an unintroduced van’t Hoff relation.
Total entropy combines the system term with surroundings heat entropy; exothermic heat alone cannot establish spontaneity at all temperatures.
At fixed temperature/pressure the most stable model phase is the one of lowest molar Gibbs energy; pairwise crossings need not be stable phase boundaries.
Powder changes exposed area, not moles of a fixed-mass carbonate; acid excess makes equal final gas amounts a stoichiometric expectation.
Temperature changes the normalised kinetic-energy distribution; a larger above-threshold fraction and collision frequency both affect successful collisions.
Catalysed and uncatalysed paths share endpoints, so both forward and reverse barriers change while enthalpy and equilibrium do not.
Adding NO2 at constant volume causes its instantaneous concentration jump, then reverse N2O4 formation; nitrogen-atom balance and K are preserved during relaxation.

Haber synthesis is exothermic; lower temperature favours equilibrium ammonia but may reduce rate, and pressure shifts depend on reacting-gas stoichiometry. No composition calculation is required at SL.
Gas-to-aqueous CO2 equilibrium responds to its own gas partial pressure, not merely total air pressure; warming opposes an exothermic dissolution.
For equal total reacting gas stoichiometry, inert gas added at fixed volume changes total pressure but not reacting partial concentrations; catalysis leaves K unchanged.
A measured zero-order consumption law gives constant concentration loss over its validated range; molecularity applies only to elementary steps and cannot be zero.
An introduced saturating empirical rate law has limiting first-order and zero-order regimes; no detailed catalytic mechanism is presumed.
A step activation barrier is measured from that step’s preceding minimum, not a global reference. Comparing speed from barrier heights also requires stated frequency/concentration assumptions.
Arrhenius slopes require absolute temperature and consistent joules with R; k ratios use the same reaction regime and concentration convention.
Linear Arrhenius intercept is the logarithm of the numerical A in the specified units; slope times−R gives activation energy.
A lower barrier can be offset by a smaller Arrhenius factor for a separate pathway; adding a parallel positive-rate pathway does not remove the original pathway.
Curved Arrhenius behaviour rejects a single constant-Ea/A model over the full range but does not identify a unique mechanism without further evidence.
A and B are isomers, so their total amount is conserved in a closed one-to-one interconversion; adding A changes total concentration but not K.
All three species are isomers of one molecular formula, so one-to-one interconversions conserve the total. Multiplying the two concentration ratios cancels the intermediate isomer B.

limitations: Author chemical/mathematical review and executable checks are not human examiner moderation. Final independent mathematical, chemical and visual audit must bind the released bytes.
